To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serotonin increases the incidence of sensory-evoked long-term plasticity in deep dorsal horn neurons, and this is mediated by serotonin receptor subtypes 1A/1b.

serotonin (5-HT) increases the incidence of sensory input-induced long-term depression (LT) in spinal cord deep dorsal horn (DH) neurons and potently depresses postconditioning sensory input-evoked responses.

serotonin (5-hydroxy-tryptamine, 5-HT) increases the incidence of long-term depression (a form of synaptic plasticity that decreases the amplitude of synaptic responses) in rat deep dorsal (spinal) horn neurons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the cellular basis of pain and how it is modulated by the central nervous system.
how the nervous system controls and modulates sensory information in order to maintain the integrity of the body.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie the modulation of sensory information in the spinal cord.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
serotonin increases the incidence of LTD, but does not affect the expression of LTP.
5-HT can depress the amplitude of sensory-evoked synaptic responses, and this can be associated with an increased probability for the induction of LTD.
5-HT depresses the amplitude of evoking synaptic input and also controls the direction of its modifiability in favor of LTD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
5-HT can both depress the synaptic input to DDH neurons and control the direction of the plasticity of that input, favoring the induction of LTD.
5-HT can depress the amplitude of sensory input and control the direction of long-term modifiabilities of synaptic input, favoring the induction of LTD.
5-HT increases the incidence of sensory input-evoked LTD and potently depresses the amplitude of postconditioning responses regardless of the direction of plasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
serotonin can not only inhibit sensory input to the dorsal horn but also can bias its long-term plasticity to favor long-term depression (i.e., the opposite of long-term potentiation).
5-HT can control both the amplitude of evocked synaptic responses and the direction of its modifiability.
serotonin can not only modulate the amplitude of sensory-evoked responses but can also control the long-term plasticity of these responses.
